title: Crown vs Filling: When You Need a Dental Crown
seoTitle: Crown vs Filling: When to Choose a Dental Crown or Filling
description: Crown vs filling: how dentists decide, when a crown protects a root-canaled tooth, typical costs and lifespans, and when a filling is enough. Valencia, CA.
excerpt: How much tooth is left, whether it had a root canal and where it sits in the bite decide between a crown and a filling. A clear comparison with typical costs and lifespans.
author: Dr. Nuriel Lavi, DDS

keyTakeaways: Fillings suit small to moderate cavities with healthy remaining walls; crowns protect teeth with major structural loss, fractures or a prior root canal.

body:
If you have a worn, broken or decayed tooth, you have probably already searched for crown vs filling. The right choice affects how long the tooth lasts, what you spend now and later, and how likely you are to avoid an emergency visit. This guide from Dr. Nuriel Lavi at Valencia Dentistry in Santa Clarita explains how dentists decide, what each option costs and when a more conservative repair makes sense. For lab-made and same-day options, see our [dental crowns](/services/dental-crowns/) service page.

Three concerns come up again and again: fear of losing a tooth after a root canal, surprise costs when a crown is added to a root canal, and confusion about when conservative treatment is appropriate. Quotes vary widely; it is not unusual for one office to price a root canal at around $600 and another at close to $1,500, with the crown adding roughly $700 to $850 or more. Dentists also use a practical rule of thumb: when a restoration would need to cover more than about one third of a cusp width, a crown is usually the safer choice.

## Crown vs filling: a clinical comparison

| Feature | Filling (direct composite or amalgam) | Crown (full coverage) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary use | Small to moderate cavities, minor fractures, cosmetic repairs | Large structural loss, after root canal therapy, fractured teeth |
| Procedure time | One visit, typically 20 to 60 minutes | Two visits for a traditional lab crown, or one visit with CAD/CAM milling; 60 to 120 or more minutes total |
| Typical lifespan | 5 to 10 years for composite; up to 10 to 15 years with excellent maintenance | 10 to 15 years or longer depending on material and habits |
| Cost range (U.S.) | $100 to $450 depending on material and size | $800 to $2,000 depending on material and lab versus in-office milling |
| When preferred | Tooth structure mostly intact and the defect is small | Multiple cusps lost, after endodontic treatment, or when fracture risk is high |

Patient resources describe similar thresholds. The American Dental Association describes fillings for small to moderate decay and crowns for larger damage or root canal protection, and the NHS notes that crowns are chosen when a large part of the tooth is missing or weakened: [ADA MouthHealthy](https://www.mouthhealthy.org) and [NHS: Dental crown](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dental-crown/).

## How dentists decide: the practical checklist

Experienced clinicians weigh structural risk, symptoms and cost. These are the decision points you will hear:

- **Amount of remaining tooth.** When more than roughly one third of a cusp, or a large area between teeth, is missing, many clinicians prefer a crown to guard against fracture.
- **Root canal status.** Teeth that have had root canal therapy are often crowned because endodontically treated teeth can be more brittle.
- **Location and bite forces.** Back teeth that carry chewing loads are more likely to need full cusp coverage than front teeth.
- **Finances and timing.** Delaying an indicated crown after a root canal is a common cause of tooth loss; patients who postpone it sometimes face extraction later.
- **Alternative restorations.** Onlays and overlays preserve more tooth than a full crown and can be a sound middle ground.

### Signs that point toward a crown

Visible cusp fractures, recurrent decay under a large filling, a tooth that needs a post after endodontic therapy, or a tooth that has fractured before are all red flags. Temporizing a root-canaled tooth with only a temporary filling can lead to a fracture that cannot be repaired, especially when the final crown is delayed for months.

### When a filling remains the right choice

Small to medium cavities with healthy remaining walls, cosmetic repairs and cases where preserving natural tooth is the priority all suit a filling. For many younger patients with sound enamel and low wear, a well-placed composite filling is the conservative choice.

## Procedure, materials and recovery

A filling takes one visit: the tooth is cleaned, decay is removed and composite is placed and cured. A crown takes more steps: tooth preparation, a digital scan or impression, a provisional and final cementation. Dr. Lavi uses an iTero digital scanner and makes custom crowns in-house, so a same-day crown is possible in many cases.

Materials matter. Composite blends with enamel but can wear faster under heavy bite forces. Porcelain and zirconia crowns offer higher strength and better long-term color stability. Gold remains an excellent, wear-friendly option on molars where appearance is not the priority. For how we choose materials, see our [services overview](/services/).

## Costs and real-world numbers

Prices vary by region, insurance and material, and the spread between quotes can be wide. The examples above, a root canal priced anywhere from about $600 to $1,475 with a crown adding $700 to $850, reflect differences in provider type, whether removal of an old crown is included and local market rates. The ranges below are typical U.S. figures, not Valencia Dentistry fees.

| Item | Typical U.S. range | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Composite filling | $100 to $450 | Depends on size and tooth location |
| Root canal (molar) | $600 to $1,500 or more | Specialist fees vary |
| Dental crown | $800 to $2,000 or more | Material and lab work drive the price |

Dental authorities place average filling life at roughly 5 to 10 years and crown longevity often beyond 10 years with good care. The National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research and the ADA patient pages offer concise summaries. For local pricing, see our [dental crowns cost guide](/dental-crowns-cost-santa-clarita-prices-guide/).

## When to get a second opinion

If you are told you need a crown but the tooth still has intact cusps, or if cost and timing force a delay after a root canal, a second opinion is reasonable. Complex endodontic or restorative cases are sometimes best referred to a specialist. If the plan includes replacing the tooth with an implant, our [dental implants vs dentures](/dental-implants-vs-dentures/) guide gives context.

## Making the decision

Crown vs filling should be decided by how much tooth remains, what the tooth does, whether a root canal was performed and your financial and timing constraints. Delaying a definitive restoration carries real risk. When in doubt, get a clinical assessment and, if recommended, a second opinion so you keep the tooth for as long as possible at a sensible cost. For a restorative evaluation in Valencia, our [dental crowns](/services/dental-crowns/) team can review your options, give a transparent estimate and discuss phased care. faq.q: When should I choose a crown instead of a filling?
faq.a: Choose a crown when the tooth has lost substantial structure, several cusps are weakened, the tooth has had a root canal, or a vertical crack threatens fracture. A common rule of thumb: if the restoration would cover more than one third of a cusp width, a crown is generally safer for long-term survival.

faq.q: Can I delay a crown after a root canal until I can afford it?
faq.a: Delaying raises fracture risk. Teeth left with only a temporary filling after root canal therapy can fracture and become unrestorable. If cost is the barrier, ask about phased care, payment plans or alternative restorations.

faq.q: How long does a crown last compared with a filling?
faq.a: A well-made crown commonly lasts 10 to 15 years or longer; fillings typically last 5 to 10 years depending on size and material. Oral hygiene, grinding and diet all affect lifespan, and regular exams catch wear before failure.

faq.q: Are onlays or overlays a good middle ground?
faq.a: Yes. Onlays and overlays preserve more natural tooth than a full crown and work well when moderate cusp coverage is needed. They are a conservative alternative when a full crown would remove healthy structure unnecessarily.

faq.q: Will a crown stop sensitivity after a root canal?
faq.a: If the sensitivity comes from structural movement or microleakage, a well-seated crown can protect the tooth and reduce discomfort. Persistent sensitivity after endodontic treatment should be evaluated for residual infection or bite issues, or referred for endodontic re-evaluation.

faq.q: Same-day milled crown or traditional lab crown?
faq.a: Same-day CAD/CAM crowns cut down on appointments and can be cost-competitive. Traditional lab crowns may offer more material choices and custom esthetics. The recommendation depends on tooth location, material needs and bite forces.
